CANADIAN UNIVERSITY SERVICE OVERSEAS TWENTIETH ANNIVERSARY-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on June 6, 1961, representatives of 21 Canadian universities and 22 non-profit organizations and churches met to found CUSO. Since then 8,000 Canadians, of all ages, have worked in developing countries, passing on skills and gaining insight from their years abroad. Today 611 volunteers serve in Africa, Asia, Latin American, the Caribbean and South Pacific. On this twentieth anniversary occasion, I move, seconded by the hon. members for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. All-mand) and Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle):
That this House recognizes that CUSO represents a high profile and important Canadian presence overseas, and that this House encourages Canadians to continue their financial and moral support for this important instrument for peace and international understanding.

subsubtopic: OUTCOME OF SALARY NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Solicitor General. It has to do with the scandalous treatment by the Treasury Board and the government of the salary question with respect to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Yesterday the minister said that the RCMP has never failed to serve the Canadian people. Given that statement, with which the House is in general agreement, does the minister not feel it is important that the RCMP be treated appropriately with respect to salaries? Given the assumption, which was in the hearts and minds even of the negotiators for the government with respect to salaries, that the increase would be effective from January 1, 1981, what does the Solicitor General intend to do to right the scandalous settlement with this group, which the minister has described as one which has never failed to serve the Canadian people?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: OUTCOME OF SALARY NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not accept the characterization of this pay increase as scandalous. It is a pay increase of 12.2 per cent plus certain other benefits, such as the achievement of full pay after 36 months for new recruits instead of after 48 months, and such as double time instead of time and a half for overtime service by members of the force on days of rest. A number of components are welcomed by the force.
The increase does not go back to January 1, and I am having discussions with the Treasury Board on that aspect of the package. However, to characterize the increase as small is totally unfair to the Treasury Board because, if we look at other pay increases the Treasury Board has accorded in the last several months, we find that this is right in line. If we compare how the police are doing with how the average Canadian is doing-and I do not think that is an invalid comparison-members of the police profession have been moving ahead, and are continuing to move ahead.
As I say, we are looking again at the three-month period, at exactly what did happen and at what undertakings were given in the past. I think members of the force themselves would have to acknowledge the facts I have indicated respecting this pay increase in relation to other pay increases. It is not bad. No one gets everything he wants from his employer, or from

June 5, 1981
Oral Questions
the Treasury Board when it is a public service matter, but if we look at this in relation to what is being done, it cannot be rejected as being scandalous.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister must be aware that there was an expectation- and he has almost acknowledged that there was an expectation-during the period of negotiations that the period under the new schedule would begin on January 1, 1981. What has happened is that there is a 12 per cent increase for a 15-month period rather than a 12 per cent increase for a 12-month period, which in effect is a reduction of what was negotiated and what was expected.
Will the minister give an undertaking to the House that he will use the procedures which are open to him, the cabinet and the Treasury Board, to effect a review of that decision by the Treasury Board, so that what is regarded generally in the force as a slap in the face, despite what the Solicitor General said, will be rectified and the matter will be put right, and so that the minister and the government will be able to live up to what the minister himself said when he characterized the Royal Canadian Mounted Police as a group which has never failed to serve the Canadian people? If that is the case, and if that is the view of the government, then the RCMP ought to be treated as such. I ask for that undertaking from the Solicitor General.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am happy to give that undertaking because, as I indicated in my first answer, that is in fact going on. However, I want to point out to the House that the Treasury Board looks at this as money. This is taxpayers' money, and if this pay increase is to go back for three additional months, from the point of view of Treasury Board and within their terms of reference, it will affect the amount of the increase in percentage terms. If the hon. member understands that, then he understands the basis on which this review is taking place.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:

We want to be fair to the RCMP, but we want to be fair in relation to all of the other pays set by the Treasury Board, and to the burden on the taxpayers. These are all considerations before us.
The RCMP have a point about making their year a calendar one, but if it is, they will be just about the only one out of 370 pays set by Treasury Board that operate on the calendar year instead of the fiscal year, which is the normal operating period of the government. These considerations are all there, but basically we are talking about taxpayers' money-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: And fairness.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: -and I would remind the House that police officers, the RCMP in particular, have been doing better than the average Canadian over the last 15 years, for example, and that is also a consideration.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: Madam Speaker, when the Attorney General of Canada receives a report from the Director of Investigation and Research, he must, after due consideration, decide whether or not to prosecute. If he does, then the report is naturally made public before the courts. If, on the other hand, he decides not to prosecute, then the report stays as is. The Director of Investigation and Research can comment on the Attorney General's action in his annual report or he can pursue the investigation if he wants to. However, the report I have received remains a privileged document between the director and the Attorney General, pursuant to the Combines Investigation Act. I know of no other precedent where a report was made public other than through a court proceeding and never was a report made public when the Attorney General ruled against prosecuting the companies or the individuals involved.

speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, my question of privilege pertains to inconsistencies with respect to rulings made by committee chairmen. It seems that what is an acceptable motion in one committee is not in another. As you, Madam Speaker, are in charge of the committee clerks, I would strongly suggest that you look into this matter and attempt to develop a system in which all clerks are consistent in the information they provide the committee chairmen.

ruling made by the chairman, the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Dupras).
I have two precedents for rising on this particular question of privilege, the first one being a motion in the communications and culture committee which passed and was reported to the House of Commons May 28, 1981.
The second precedent was a motion which passed and was reported to the House Friday, February 28, 1969, from the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates. I am sure Your Honour will want to look at these motions. I will not take the time to read them into the record now. The ruling by Mr. Speaker Lamoureux on a challenge to this motion occurred Monday, June 18, 1973. The Speaker upheld the prior motion. In doing that the Speaker said:

The first example of such a report was that of the fourth report of the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates made February 28, 1969, concerning the use of one-dollar items for the purpose of legislating. That report followed upon the adoption of the revised rules in December 1968.
Last Thursday I presented a motion in the veterans affairs committee with regard to a very serious problem concerning the processing of pensions. It takes one to five years to process these.
What recourse do I have because a clerk made an error in committee? This should not restrict my functioning as a member of Parliament in committees. Can this motion be made retroactive due to the seriousness of the problem caused by the clerk and chairman of that committee?

That does not address itself to the particular problem which the hon. member has, but the time to seek the redress he is asking for is when there is a motion for concurrence in the House on that report. speechtext: The House resumed, from Tuesday, April 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bussieres that Bill C-58, to amend the Canada Elections Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful to have this opportunity to rise to comment on Bill C-58. I have been waiting for a long time to have introduced the platform on which one could build a number of reforms that are obviously required in our Canada Elections Act.
Each time I have submitted myself to the electorate of Esquimalt-Saanich for election I have discovered a number of, perhaps not abuses or improprieties, but shortcomings in the act, and on each occasion I have prepared for my own use and for the use of my party a summary of the shortcomings that occurred to me and the group that was working with me during the election so that one might have at hand a full list of these various shortcomings.
June 5, 1981

I think basically the best time for a discussion or a debate on electoral reform is immediately after an election when matters are still fresh in one's mind. In the absence of the ability to call that debate so soon after an election, the best we can do is make use of this opportunity, and each opportunity that does present itself, to raise during the general discussion at second reading those problems and shortcomings which have occurred and manifested themselves during an election campaign.
I have a long list, seven, eight or nine of them. In the most recent election I suppose I added several. In my first election I was not all that sure and was not able to compare it with any previous experience. In my second election I was able to see there were shortcomings, and now, following my fourth election in February, 1980, I have made a list of those shortcomings.
Bill C-58 is designed primarily to deal with shortening of the election period. It does deal with other matters, of course. There are some very narrow administrative matters connected with the shortening of the period, limitation of the number of copies of the list and maps, and we hear about things that ought to be at the polling stations, including one copy of the preliminary list of electors for every polling division comprised in his revisal district, and so on. This is an administrative matter too, but I have a suggestion to make about that as well.
There is reference to election day and the returning officers transmitting notices of grants of polls, combining urban advanced polling districts and so on. I do feel on the strength of that that it is possible to make a very broad comment on a number of matters relating to that period when elections take place, now a matter of some 59 days, and not just confine my remarks to the preparation of the electoral rolls.
My first comments, however, are going to be concerned with the preparation of the electoral roll. My suggestion-I have made it before in committee and I am going to put it on the record again-is for the establishment of a permanent voters' list. We do need a permanent voters' list. It is crucial to the whole matter of shortening the election period, if that should be the desire of the House. It is certainly the desire of the government or it would not have brought forward a motion containing this shortening from 59 to 47 days. In my view there ought to be, and there certainly is in certain provinces of Canada, certainly in British Columbia, a permanent voters' list.
This matter has been explored in other countries. Perhaps the argument is that there are too many dead people on the lists, that their names are not struck off before the election period and that someone will vote for them. I feel that in a democracy as mature as that in our country we should be able to have confidence that our fellow citizens will make sure they are not voting twice or that they are not voting on behalf of a dead relative who happens to be on the list. There are means of checking that. Even with the mobility of the population of Canada today I think one could devise a number of ways of
Canada Elections Act
making sure that a permanent voters' list is kept up to date. It would not be a very difficult matter, as I see it.
We might have provision within the law for a check of the voters' list on the second day of January and the second day of July. Perhaps it should be mandatory for people who have moved since the previous registration date to amend the permanent voters' list. This could be done in municipal offices. The list could be used for other purposes as well, but I think there ought to be a check twice a year.
There should also be checks x number of days after election writs are issued just to be sure that the list is brought even more up to date. Perhaps it should be law that January 2 and July 2 are designated as days on which people make sure their names are on the voters' list. With present technology and computerization I see no reason in the world why it should not be possible to have a permanent voters' list and why we cannot be sure that when election writs are issued the list can just be run off and sent to the printers. In this case we are not talking about printers but about instant print reproduction facilities. In this way the voters' list would be available to those who need it during election campaigns. As hon. members know, many people need voters' lists. If they are available on a permanent basis, that might be very helpful.
A census is presently being taken. A voters' list might be very helpful to census takers when they are updating and forecasting mobility within the country. I foresee a variety of uses to which a permanent voters' list could be put, and those uses are aside altogether from the essential nature of a voters' list. I do believe a voters' list would be an essential tool for a well-run election.
Another matter was on my mind during the last election campaign. It has to do with the problem brought about by people who make holiday plans based on discount air fares which are now available if people book well in advance. Sometimes bookings have to be made three months, four months or five months in advance, before there is any notion that there is to be an election. People decide to take holidays at certain times in order to take advantage of excursion fares which are offered by a number of airlines. These people book in advance and make down payments. Sometimes they make the whole payment and get a special advantage. Then an election comes along, and it is held right in the middle of people's holidays. Such people find that they lose their right to vote on election day and that the provision for advance polling is not adequate.
I think there should be greater flexibility in returning offices respecting early voting. I admit that there already is some flexibility; however, a returning officer very kindly sent his comments about this to me. He says he is a little worried about extended voting in the offices of returning officers. I wonder why he should be worried. If it is a matter of space or staff, if we had a permanent voters' list well in place right at the beginning of an election period, there ought not to be any great problem having people working and having people voting in returning offices. I think the misgivings expressed by the returning officer in his letter, a copy of which I have in my

June 5, 1981
Canada Elections Act
hand, are premised on the notion that the prevailing regime with respect to voters' lists will be carried forward into the next election.
In any event, if there is provision in the law for advance voting during most of the period of an election, as soon as the list is available there should be accommodation so that voters can come in and vote. Of course, they should have to prove that they will not be available to vote on election day. They should have to give just cause for advance voting, but they should be offered the opportunity to vote at the returning office during the major portion of an election period.
Another matter which worries me somewhat is the matter of proxy voting. I think we need an enlargement of the classes of persons and a simplification of procedures governing those who may vote by proxy. As hon. members know, at the present time a person may proxy for only one voter. I will be making a suggestion about having polling stations in nursing homes and so forth. It may be that in some areas mobile polling booths are not practical. Therefore, it should be possible, for example, for the matron of a nursing home, a doctor on duty or someone responsible for the care of individuals in a nursing home to be given a proxy vote in order to vote on behalf of those who are immobilized in the nursing home. I see no reason why it should not be possible for one person to vote by proxy for several others. Are we afraid that people will take advantage of this and invent people on behalf of whom they can vote? That is possible, but if that is the situation, I think it is a sad comment on our electoral system. As I say, I believe there is room for enlarging the class of persons and the number of persons for whom proxy votes can be cast.
This brings me to another important matter which I raised in a private members' bill as long ago as the Twenty-ninth or Thirtieth Parliament. During my second term of office I became aware in a real way of the difficulties which can occur when people cannot get out to vote either at advance polls or on polling days. In all constituencies there are persons who, through no fault of their own, have great difficulty getting out to vote or finding proxies.
My suggestion was shot down by the Chief Electoral Officer at the time. I managed to get it as far as the committee where I fought for it and defended it, but where it was turned down. I have some reason to suspect now, Mr. Speaker, that the Chief Electoral Officer may have modified his views and would be prepared to accept this notion. With all due respect, I think it is for Parliament, not the Chief Electoral Officer, to decide whether there shall be mobile polling stations. Therefore, I feel we should more fully explore this notion of a mobile ballot box for hospitals, shut-ins in nursing homes and, particularly as this is the International Year of the Handicapped, the disabled.
It is a simple matter, as 1 see it. The poll clerk and scrutineers would be available, they could travel around in a mobile van which could be rented on the day of the vote, or even I suggest for an advance poll. I see there are some smiles
on the other side; perhaps they can see some way of sneaking around some of these suggestions which I am making in all honesty. I see no reason why a group of four or five persons in a small van, fully equipped, could not visit the hospitals and actually go into the hospital room and have the person, even those immobilized in bed, mark the ballot. I cannot understand what this smirking is about on the other side. It can only be imagination about machinations, I think. So I would revive that matter as one which I consider worth exploring more fully, and in the course of time I hope I might have the opportunity to introduce an amendment to that effect to this bill.
Another matter involves visiting polling stations on voting day to see if there are any problems and, if not, just to say hello to people. There are some who may do other things on voting day but I have made it a practice to be of service to the community and to visit as many polling stations as I could within the area. Now some, such as my friend, the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle), would be unable to visit all the polling stations in their riding in one day. However, in mostly urban, slightly rural, constituencies such as mine it is possible to visit at least half, I would say.
One of the problems I find when I do this is that people show up because they live nearby, they see the polling station on their way to work and so they say this is where the vote is going to take place and they walk in expecting to be able to vote. It may just be that they are in the wrong polling station, they may have moved six months ago from the place where their name is on the list and they really have to go some distance away. I have suggested to polling officers, and also to the electoral officer of the riding, that he provide to each polling station a map showing the locations of the stations in the ridings in some detail. If the people chosen as scrutineers really had their wits about them and they made sure that maps were available, when people came in they could look at the map and say to the people concerned: "Look, that is where you live and this is where the poll is in that particular riding; you go down this street, turn right, follow the streetcar tracks and you will get there". I do think that is an important service.
I also think it is very important that there should be available in polling stations a full voters' list so that people can check to see whether they are on the list and which poll they would vote at. There is a practice in some constituencies, I believe, to send out what are known as vote-at cards. These are rather difficult to organize at the last minute no matter how many people you have to do it. It is also a little dangerous because there is a temptation to put a little bit of advertising on these cards and then, of course, the voter walks into the polling station with your card in his hand and this gets pretty close to the bounds of illegality and could thereby get you into difficulty. In my riding we decided in the last four elections that we would not issue these cards for that very reason. Despite the best will in the world, people will pull this out of their pocket and say this is where I go to vote, and then you have your picture there with the space to mark the ballot and
June 5, 1981

so on, which is, of course, a no-no. And so it should be; I have no quarrel with that at all.
However, we must try to overcome difficulties that people have. People have other things to think about than that single day. After all, the candidates have focused on that single day, but the rest of the voting population, or a large part of them, are focusing on getting their daily bread, as they do on other days. Therefore, while they are determined to get to the polling station, they may make a mistake as to where they should go, so I feel there ought to be all the necessary facilities within each polling station to enable a voter to find his way to the right polling station.
The alternative, I suppose, would be to put his vote in a jumbo box and strike his name off the voters' lists then rush to the phone and make sure that the appropriate polling station strikes his name off the list. But I think that is too complicated. I think the best way is to provide a service which will enable people to find their way to the appropriate polling station.
There is another matter which struck me as very odd; 1 cannot understand the rationale behind it. A rural voter may go the the polling station on voting day with a neighbour and swear himself for inclusion on the electoral list. An urban voter may not. Perhaps an urban voter is not supposed to have a neighbour. A rural voter may have a friend or neighbour accompany him to the polling station in order to swear before the poll clerk that indeed the person has been living at a certain address in the rural riding for a number of weeks, months or whatever it is. If a rural voter whose name does not appear on the list can place it on the list in such a fashion, why is it not possible to have the same facility for an urban voter? It just does not make sense.
I suppose it stems from historical usage. Perhaps it is "historical abusage", I am not sure. In the early days of voting, the facilities for communication were not what they are today. I can visualize the set-up in the rural areas of the prairies, particularly. A farmer who is busy with his crops cannot get away from the farm because of the weather. He can be busy with his livestock or his family and cannot get away during that narrow period so that his name will be included on the voters' list. He could make arrangements in advance to have his stock watered or his cows milked, if that is the case, so that he would accompany a neighbour on election day to have his name included on the list. This is the possible historic explanation; there cannot be any other. Therefore, I feel there is a good argument in favour of extending this facility to urban voters. Of course, this is the permanent list of which I spoke earlier.
I should like to turn to a somewhat more subtle area, that of the screening of returning officers. Heretofore they have been appointed because of political affiliation. Then it is more or less a permanent appointment. If their performance is good, they will just stay on or remain in office.
Canada Elections Act
Certain stories reach us immediately after an election campaign which happily are forgotten 15 or 16 months after the election. These stories concern bias displayed by returning officers or conflicts of interests which suggest that perhaps there was an inclination to guide an elector in one direction or another or to make decisions which adversely affect one candidate as against another. I know there are provisions within the bill for appeal both during the election period and after, but it would be much better if we could be absolutely clear on this matter and not have the problem arise at all. My suggestion is that there might be a need for screening returning officers for conflicts of interest which might be evident or for political bias.
An interesting matter was the subject of a letter which appeared in The Times-Colonist in Victoria last month. I suppose this comes back to the matter I raised concerning mobile ballot boxes. I should like to read this short letter. It deserves to be put on the record because it underlines the need to help those people who find themselves unable to get to the polls on voting day. The letter does not include any address. This person may be speaking for herself or on behalf of others. I do not want to embarrass the author of the letter; therefore, I will not use her name. The letter reads as follows:
It seems that I and other shut-ins are second-rate citizens. Believe it or not, in Canada we are not able to vote. Oh, sure, we can vote by proxy, but I don't want to and I shouldn't have to. My vote is supposed to be secret. How can it be if I tell another person? I want and demand my constitutional right to vote. Surely this great government can arrange to have ballot boxes brought around to shut-ins' homes.
I talked about nursing homes and hospitals. I agree that there are homes and apartments where people are shut in or unable to move because of handicaps. Those people ought to have their secrecy preserved; they should be able to vote.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
I have suggested that with mobile voting stations there should be no problem, even if it takes three or four days. Gracious goodness, with our facilities we should be able to work out some system whereby people who cannot get to voting stations can vote two or three days beforehand and have their votes locked up to be counted on voting day. I am delighted to see that there was a positive response on the other side of the House to this notion. I do not want to see the secrecy of the vote denied to anyone. We ought to show them respect, whether they are confined because of illness or handicap. In this year in particular I think we should be thinking of the handicapped. When a person is sick in bed, I suppose it is a handicap as well. We must find a way of overcoming this problem.
There is some suggestion in the bill about the need to avoid the lengthy process of printing and using copy houses which permits the photostatic method of reproducing the electoral roll. This has been considered by some. I sent a copy of the bill when it was printed to the returning officer in my riding in order for his comments. He appropriately replied to the Chief Electoral Officer and sent me a copy of the letter which he wrote. He indicated that he was delighted there was an extra

June 5, 1981
Canada Elections Act
facility which meant that he would not have to take the voters' list to a print shop where it must be typeset, which takes a fair amount of time. This is no reflection on the typesetters; it is just a matter of time since it could be reproduced by the electrostatic method.
He does comment about having the returning office opened up for a longer period than in the past-21 days instead of 14-so that people could come in and vote. I think 1 have covered this matter. I can see no reason in the world why, if necessary, the returning office cannot be a little shop, or an office at the back or front end of a shop, which would be manned at all times by a returning officer and his staff. I am sure all parties would be delighted to change scrutineers, from day to day if necessary, so that when people did come in for an advance poll it would be possible for them to vote.
One other matter which caused concern in the 1979 election, one which I suspect may arise again, was that there were a great many people caught by surprise because of the change of designation. There were a number of British subjects who had voted in the past and they were warned that if they did not become Canadian citizens and get their names on to the voters' list they would find they might be denied the right to vote. Indeed, I think all members sent out notices with our householders' mailing indicating this change.
It must be borne in mind that these people have been in this country for a good many years, with their children and their grandchildren, many of whom were born here. They had assumed that they were Canadian citizens and they were rather affronted, if not insulted, when they found they were not, just by the effluxion of time, considered Canadian citizens. Some of them may have lost their ability to vote. At the time this caused a great deal of hard feeling. If that provision is within the Canada Elections Act I think it would be worth while to take a closer look at it in committee.
I see that you are indicating to me that my time has almost expired, Mr. Speaker. I want to thank you for bearing with me as I have gone through these various matters which have been concerns of mine in each election. I am glad that the opportunity is before us now to consider this matter. I hope it will be possible to open up this bill and add to it amendments which will rectify some of the shortcomings, as I have decided to call them, of the previous acts.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as 1 mentioned, I welcome this bill and the idea that we can shorten our election campaigns from 60 days to 47 days. I am sure that this idea is a welcome one in my riding in Mississauga as well. I see the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) here. When he spoke on this bill in April, he wondered if we could make it retroactive to 16 election campaigns!

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: My first campaign was in 1980, but it was my eighth campaign involved with Liberal party politics.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
I have been an organizer and a volunteer in eight federal campaigns since 1963. In each campaign I have been struck by the fact that it is getting easier and easier, from the politician's perspective, to shorten campaigns. I refer to both our national and our local campaigns.
Nationally, of course, since 1963, when I got started, we have seen the advent of better and better air and jet travel. Jet aircraft are being used for leaders' campaigns and for the media, taking our leaders right across the country so that they can speak in any corner at any given time during the campaign. Because of good television coverage, they are able to be reported right across the nation; and with increasingly sophisticated advertising techniques, we are able to carry our own biased or political messages right across the country.
At the local level, we have seen the same kind of changes since I got started in 1963. We have seen, for example, that we now include the party name on the ballot so that candidates do not have to spend so long identifying themselves with the national message that the national media and the national leadership are carrying to the voters. We see that there is much less focus on local meetings and local debate; we see, instead, at least in the areas where I have had experience, that people are campaigning more in shopping plazas, along streets and door to door. I think all of this makes our local and our national canjpaign much more flexible and much easier to shorten.
I welcome this bill, but as we look at it, I think we have to apply three principles and see if the bill passes the test. First of all, we have to ask, is the bill fair to everyone; not only fair to every party, but fair to the incumbent and the challenger? We have to make sure that the large numbers of people who are waiting outside this House to replace us are at least given a fair chance, if not a lot of encouragement.
June 5, 1981

Second, we have to look to see whether this bill will encourage greater efficiency in our electoral system. We do not just want to look at a hypothetical public attention span. We also want to look at our officials and the people who are the referees in elections to make sure that they agree with this measure.
Third, because I think that in this kind of an arrangement appearances are everything, we want to make sure that there is consensus among all the parties. This bill comes from two previous bills. It has a non-partisan atmosphere attached to it and it is of a housekeeping nature.
In a 1975 report on the 1974 election, the Chief Electoral Officer made a recommendation to the then president of the privy council, Mr. Sharp, that we shorten campaigns. Following that, a bill was introduced by the previous Liberal administration. Another bill was introduced by the previous Clark administration. The report to which I have just referred was tabled in the House in 1976.
The Chief Electoral Officer divided our election campaigns into three distinct periods of time. From his point of view, these are three distinct activities. The most important stage was the last stage, that is the last 30 days when we are getting ready for the actual balloting. This is when we see the candidates nominated, ballots printed and distributed in the proper numbers, local officials recruited and trained and the advance polls and regular polls opened and operating properly.
The Chief Electoral Officer made the point in his report that this is a period we cannot shorten nor alter in any way.' This last 30-day effort should not be interfered with. Therefore, he examined the first two stages in the first 30 days of our current electoral campaign. This is when people are enumerated, when lists are published and errors and omissions are corrected. The electoral officer found plenty of room for improvement in this area. He was able to recommend two things. He recommended, first, that the period be shortened by 13 days, from 60 days to 47 days; second, that there was a new way to treat voters' lists which would save $2 million in 1974 dollars, a welcome saving and a sizeable amount at any time.
Since that time there has been considerable support for this idea, that is to say, that we shorten our campaigns. I obtained four newspaper clippings through our library services. I think they quite well represent public opinion. The first one is dated February 3, 1981, after we reintroduced this bill, an editorial article in the Star Phoenix, which reported the following:
Even a minimum of 47 days appears to be too long in this age of speed in communication with voters.
On February 11, 1981 the Chronicle-Herald underlined the same idea. We read in its article the following:
The bill should be put through and made ready for the next election, and not allowed to be withdrawn for consideration in another session.
And while the MPs are at it, perhaps they might consider further reducing the time allotted for campaigning.
Canada Elections Act
These two newspapers expressed opinions that they were not happy even with the 47-day period allowed in this bill, that the period should be shorter.
Following the 1980 campaign, under the title of "electoral reform", the Winnipeg Free Press, in an article written on February 18, 1980, expressed this thought:
This time, Canadians, by accident, had a campaign of more nearly European length with no ill effects.
The article continued:
No one could seriously complain that, in the six weeks they gave themselves, the parties did not have an opportunity to get their messages across to the public. Indeed, the job could have been done quite adequately in a couple of weeks less.
Those three opinions reflect reaction to this bill and to the 1980 campaign, which was quite a short campaign. After the 1979 campaign, which we all recall was a long and prolonged affair, particularly with the preparation leading up to it, the Toronto Star reported on May 24, 1979:
Shorter, sharper election campaigns would benefit Canadian democracy by concentrating debate and focusing public attention on the issues and policies involved.
I agree with the opinions expressed in those newspapers. If hon. members go through the clippings which the library provided to me, there are plenty more sentiments like that in newspapers from across the country, all of them urging us to shorten campaigns and to act expeditiously.
I think these newspaper articles reflect public opinion in two ways. I think the newspapers quite rightly see the current length of our campaigns as wasteful. These articles also show that shorter campaigns would be equally effective and equally fair.
Speaking on behalf of our audience, that is our voters, they do not believe there is any element of unfairness if we shorten our campaigns. But this question of fairness versus efficiency has to be considered pretty seriously.
The Chief Electoral Officer has told us how to shorten our election campaigns so that the process itself, the mechanics, is fair. If we follow this method, he says that voters will get listed properly, that there will still be plenty of time for correction of errors and omissions, that we would still be able to have open and proper nomination procedures, and that our balloting will continue to be scrupulously conducted by well-trained local officials.
In short, our referee will be properly conducting the match according to all the rules that we consider decent and proper. If we accept the advice of the newspapers in addition, our audience will be more than satisfied. Forty seven days will give everybody more than enough time. Our audience will see the process is fair as well.
I am trying to stress that fairness cannot be taken in isolation; it has to be balanced against efficiency. Both the Chief Electoral Officer and the newspaper critics, who have been following our habits as politicians, are saying that we can get along much faster without sacrificing fairness. We can be more efficient without being unfair.

June 5, 1981
Canada Elections Act
The third principle that we have to look at is the question of consensus. What is the status of that? I think we have to have agreement from most parties in order to proceed with this bill. The public has to see that parties of all sides think that it is a good idea. So far since April we have heard from five speakers on this bill. I think they have been in agreement in principle. We have heard from representatives of one Ontario rural riding, one Toronto urban riding, an Ottawa suburban riding, a Winnipeg urban riding, and today a B.C. riding. Each member has indicated his general agreement with the idea that we can shorten our election campaigns.
We know that the bill was introduced by both a Liberal and a Conservative administration. There were, however, two important questions raised by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) when he spoke in mid-April. On April 14, at page 9282 of Hansard, the hon. member wonders whether urban ridings might find a short campaign a little easier than a suburban riding and even easier than a widely spread rural riding. A couple of pages later the hon. member raises a second important question, whether the method favours incumbents. I shall examine those two concerns because I think they are honest questions. I would like to give the hon. member my impressions as to how we should treat his two questions.
I remember working in the Manitoba provincial campaign in 1977, a campaign which took six weeks to conduct from start to finish. The Churchill riding is enormous; it is almost as big as the federal seat. It cost approximately $2,000 for the candidate to fly around the riding just once. The riding stretched north of Flin Flon across to Churchill and it took in a lot of the geography north of Lake Winnipeg. It was filled with tiny hamlets with 100 to 200 people living next to a lake. The candidate would fly in on a float plane, visit them and then go on to the next spot. He built up an organization in each of those municipalities as he went through. I am happy to report that the mechanics of the campaign went very smoothly.
[DOT] (M20)
I watched his efforts closely. I was intrigued by the way he was going to operate. With the use of aircraft and sometimes with the use of canoes, he was able to visit personally every little hamlet at least once. He got to the bigger places twice. Through radio, television and local newspapers he was able to advertise his campaign, tell people what his platform was, what his background was and what the party generally was promoting across the province. In six weeks I did not see any way that he suffered as a result of its being a large constituency. Even though it was a provincial campaign, I believe his constituency was larger than most of those represented in this House, with the exception of those in schedule 3 of the act. As I mentioned, he got to the larger centres at least twice. He had the provincial leader in there twice.
Unfortunately, at the end of the campaign he only collected 12 per cent of the vote. That was not his fault. It was the fault of those of us sitting in Winnipeg. He convinced me in that experience that technology for travel and communication
made a modern local campaign highly effective. If you look at the result, the 12 per cent of the vote he received, it would appear that technology and travel make a provincial or national campaign highly effective. He got a pattern of the vote remarkably similar to the pattern obtained in most other ridings across Manitoba by the Liberal party in that election.
I do not want to make too much of one example, but I think it is illustrative. It is a practical example that helps us to see that travel by aircraft in remote places is often as effective as a car or walking in a crowded urban centre. He certainly got to all his constituents.
The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton asked about suburban places. I feel very confident replying to him and telling him about my own experience because I come from a suburban city west of Toronto. We have 93,000 voters and 400 polls. There are 55,000 households in my riding which is about the equivalent number of voters in smaller constituencies.
My riding is made up of people from all backgrounds and all kinds of living circumstances. They are in apartment buildings, subdivisions, instant villages and towns and historic little centres. Malton and Streetsville are there, towns which started up in the middle of the 1800s. Meadowvale, a town which started five or six years ago, is also there.
In 44 days, between January 5, 1980, when I was nominated, and February 18, when the election was held, we recruited 650 to 700 workers. We canvassed every poll in the middle of the winter. We put up over 4,000 lawn signs and conducted two mailings. I ran my own personal campaign. Some would say that was the weakest part of the effort. We went to 16 different local meetings that had been organized by schools, churches and ratepayers groups. If at the end of that effort someone did not know about my campaign, it was more accidental than purposeful. It was not a result of the time allowed, 44 days. My opponents did the same and they did it in the same time period.
In 1979, the campaigns in my constituency were conducted with the same intensity. It was spring, not winter, but the campaigns were no tougher. They were prolonged, but they were no better. My opponent in 1980 was an incumbent. He had been a challenger in 1979. He had been nominated in 1978 and had spent a year or a year and a half knocking on the 55,000 doors in our riding. Once the bell went, he did the same things as the Hon. Tony Abbott, my predecessor. He canvassed every poll, put up thousands of lawn signs and he defeated Mr. Abbott. He did it with a highly effective campaign that was dragged out from 1978 through 1979. His result was the same as mine. His took a year and a half, mine took 44 days.
I have had personal experience in a surburban area, and in northern Manitoba I witnessed with great interest a campaign. The key was the issues, personalities and the parties, not the length of time. I want to make that point quite strongly. We want to be able to say that time does not necessarily penalize people if they come from bigger areas, wilderness areas, spread out or heavily populated areas. A long campaign will not necessarily help the candidate.
June 5, 1981

Does a short campaign help an incumbent? That is the question asked by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton. It is a very important question. Do shorter campaigns create advantages for those of us here? Again I will refer back to my own riding. If ever there was a long campaign, it was the one in 1979. The local Conservative challenger at that time started in 1978. He succeeded. In 1980, with 44 days, I succeeded.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: Obviously personalities don't matter.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
I hear my neighbour for Etibocoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) making a few comments in agreement on this. I appreciate his support.
The same kinds of examples are everywhere. In 1979 the Liberals lost. In 1980 the Liberals won. Long campaigns and short campaigns did not make any difference. In both cases incumbents fell, challengers rose and governments changed. Personalities, parties and issues were the key, not the length of time.
The questions of geography and incumbency that the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton raised are answered by those parallels from the 1979 and 1980 campaigns. Look at those two elections which happened so closely together. One was long planned and the other spontaneous. If we look at the similar campaign techniques used in two different campaigns with different issues and different problems for the voters to solve, we see that, by and large, the campaign techniques themselves were not the key. The issues, personalities and substances of the campaigns made the difference.
The inquiries by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton are important. We have to satisfy those inquiries in our own minds and for the sake of those who come after we change the law. We must have a proper answer for those people as well. We have to draw a distinction between creating a fair opportunity, on the one hand, and reacting to people who do or do not take advantage of that opportunity, on the other.
We here cannot be responsible for making other people good campaigners. We can look at the outside world and determine that technology, communications and modern campaign techniques work in favour of shorter campaigns. We can make that decision. We can also decide that a 47-day campaign is a fair opportunity. There will be some who argue with us and there will be some who, if they had a hundred years, could not get elected. We are not responsible for those people.
In 1896 Tarte helped Laurier to get elected. He said at that time that elections are not won by prayer alone. In the same way, elections are not won by opportunity alone. We make the opportunity. Others will take advantage of it.
I have tried to stress in my speech that there are three principles we have to apply to any change in the electoral law. First, we have to see whether it is fair. Second, we have to see whether it is efficient. Third, we have to see whether there is general agreement among the responsible parties that we should progress.
Canada Elections Act
I do not think this should become a partisan issue. I think in terms of fairness I have tried to express that the referee, the Chief Electoral Officer, tells us that if we follow this legislation we will have a fair process, a fair administration. As far as he is responsible, he has told us that this legislation has elements of fairness in it.
Second, our audience is telling us that it would be fair and adequate to shorten our campaigns. They are saying through the newspapers-and I think the newspapers are speaking on behalf of their readers-that 47 days is long enough and we do not need to drag ourselves out even longer. Third, are the players, ourselves. I think we are seeing increasingly an agreement here. We have heard five speakers, and I am the sixth, and all of us have said we agree that campaigns should be shorter, even if there have been some queries about how we accomplish it.
I think the fairness question is settled. On the efficiency question, there is an obvious attraction. There is an attraction for politicians everywhere in cutting 25 per cent off the length of a campaign. We are now dealing with election expenditure limits and if we can cut 25 per cent off the time, then those limits will become even more generous and we might find ways to save within those limits. Certainly the public is going to save. The public has been told by the Chief Electoral Officer that in 1974 dollars we will save $2 million in the printing of the lists alone. I think that efficiency is worth pursuing even if the parties as private groups do not find efficiencies of their own.
Finally, on the third principle, the consensus principle I think is being reached here. We have seen the bill come from both sides of the House. We have heard a positive speech from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I think we have some details we can satisfy in this debate, but I think the quickest way we can show consensus is by putting the bill into the committee, getting it out of the committee, voting on it and putting it into place, which is what I think the public and all our audiences want us to do.

Mr. Speaker, this has been a subject matter with which I have had some experience, having been engaged in some ten elections, and it is an item which is of very major concern to me. I can agree with the hon. member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) in most of what he said, except that I would have to say that I think it is the prerogative of any party to nominate anybody at any point in time that it chooses, and in this political structure of ours I do not think we should be complaining because one guy had 18 months and another guy had only 47 days. That is not pertinent at all. No matter what the act may be, there will still be that prerogative to do just that. Certainly the public or any party in this House would not prevent any change which would constrict the time of nomination and thus the time of the election campaign conducted by an early nominee.
As for the time of the campaign, I think that in virtually any constituency, the time is adequate, except for some of those in

June 5, 1981
Canada Elections Act
the very large constituencies, such as Yukon, the Prince George-Peace River and the Peace River constituencies in Alberta, and others which are nearly equally as large. I do not know whether you would ever have time to cover those constituencies in any time frame. If there are hardships which would be imposed by a restriction of time, they would be the ones which would really feel it at its worst.
It does seem to me that if other jurisdictions, such as, let us say, the United Kingdom, can conduct an election in 28 days, surely Canada could stand a reduction to something like 45, plus or minus a day or two, as this bill is now proposing.
There are, however, some frailties in the act as it presently exists. I do not wish to be construed in this instance as speaking with any political malevolence at all, but I would like to see a better elections act, particularly as it relates to a rural constituency. It is in that frame of mind that I want to make a few suggestions.
For instance, the restrictions upon advertising for a convention in a rural constituency impose restraints and constraints which I do not think should be there. I think one should be permitted, as a political party or as an aspiring candidate prior to his official entry into the race, to advertise as one sees fit. I say that because I do not know how you are going to scatter the name through a community 200, 300, 500 miles in length if you do not have the opportunity to advertise.
If you are an incumbent member and you are the only candidate at a convention, I can see that it does give you some advantage. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Mississauga North, there are advantages and disadvantages. But if you are opposing an existing member, one of the advantages I think a new face in a campaign requires is the opportunity to advertise in pursuit of the nomination, and to advertise the meeting at which he hopes he may be the successful candidate. To include this in the cost of an election, or even to preclude the possibility of publicizing his name and ambitions, I think is a most unfair restriction.
If it were-and this, I suppose, is political-the intention of the government to pursue these constraints and make sure they were exercised with equal hardship on all candidates, that would be fine; but in my experience in the last two elections in this nation that has not been the case. It appears that liberties have been extended to candidates, perhaps I should say of all parties, and there has been no inclination by the Chief Electoral Officer or the returning officer to really see that this facet of the requirement of the elections act is enforced. I think we should either eliminate constraints upon advertising for a convention, or there should be a notice to all parties, to all returning officers and to all known or prospective candidates that, if they breach the law, they shall not be eligible to participate in the election.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make one or two points in relation to this item. For many years the practice in the British House of Commons and in most legislatures, if not all, in this country has been that at second reading of a bill debate is on the principle of the bill. The principle of a bill involves more than just the clauses of the bill. If that were not so, when a government introduces a bill, debate would be confined. Zippers would actually be put on the lips of members.
If Your Honour will just hear me out, when a bill is introduced, the government knows that there is open debate at second reading. In committee of the whole hon. members are confined to individual clauses. At the third reading stage hon. members can attempt to defeat the whole bill, but the only stage at which hon. members can deal with the principle of a bill is at the second reading stage. The principle of a bill involves more than just the particular clauses. The principle of this bill involves the Canada Elections Act, and I contend that if the ruling is that we must confine ourselves to clauses, we are running a committee of the whole at the second reading stage, which is definitely wrong.

If we are going to cut the time, it is imperative that the Chief Electoral Officer put everything required in place on the first go around. I do not want to have to make three trips again, nor do I wish to impose that upon any candidate who may succeed me. If there is to be a constraint in time, it would be a very excellent idea if the deputy returning officer in the advance poll could almost automatically become an appointee of the returning officer in a rural constituency to receive and perhaps to make available those votes required in proxy or absentee voting or from disabled voters. If the House will just bear with me a minute, I will not take much time-

What I am suggesting is that attempting a snip, when really what the government is planning to do is to destroy the whole animal, is ridiculous and we should not even be discussing this matter. However, it is before us and there are a number of comments that must be made relevant to this particular piece of minor legislation.
Now I can become slightly non-partisan and point out that the length of elections in Canada now runs 59 to 60 days. Every province in the country has made changes. In Newfoundland, it is 21 days for an election; Prince Edward Island, 26 days; New Brunswick, 36 days; Quebec, 32 days; Ontario, 37 days; Manitoba, 35 days; Saskatchewan, 28 days; Alberta, 29 days; British Columbia, 38 days.
If we really look at the 1980 election, we find that the writ went out on December 13. The election campaign, particularly in city ridings, did not get under way until early in January when the children went back to school. I do not think many members were out knocking on doors and saying, "Merry Christmas, please vote for me". If they did, perhaps they are not here.
The length of time of an election is only one small issue in terms of the entire question of electoral reform. This bill should not be before us at this time; it should have been held back. In approximately three months, in September, the report of the Chief Electoral Officer on the changes he wants in election law will be available.

June 5, 1981
Canada Elections Act
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said he has some major changes he wants to make. Why should we be bothered with this minor matter which ties in with every change that may be advocated in Parliament in terms of an election? Will 47 days be enough? I do not know because I do not know what are the other considerations. They are asking me to buy this pig in a poke and to decide that the election period should be shorter, without telling me what else they have planned or what other major items they will attempt to foist on Canadians. Until I am told those things, how can I possibly talk about 47 days or about electoral lists which will no longer be printed but will be mimeographed? These matters should not be before the Elouse at the moment; it is a waste of time.
Why was a committee not set up for this matter and all other changes considered at the same time? Why was there not an omnibus bill? Why have they not brought it all in? Why have we not had a chance to look at everything?
There is a stack of bills which are waiting. Various matters are involved. Some of them are good; perhaps some of them are not so good. Every one of them has some relationship to the legislation before us. When they talk about 47 days, they should realize that they are changing every facet of the Canada Elections Act. This 47 days makes a difference to the Canada Elections Act, as does the question of the printed list.
For example, the hours the polls are open might be irrelevant, but moving after the list is out is relevant to the 47 days, as is voting by proxy. Holding the level of the membership of the House to a particular figure is relevant to 47 days; perhaps it will mean many more voters in individual ridings. Will the candidates have a chance to talk to everyone involved? There is some doubt about that.
There are ridings in British Columbia which are over 500 miles long. The government should talk to members representing those ridings to hear what they have to say about the 47 days. Will they be able to get around those ridings within 47 days? I realize that originally the length of an election was established based on the difficulties of travelling by horse drawn wagons on muddy roads. Even though it was done in that manner, the distance in those early days were much shorter. The difficulties in terms of travelling about ridings in the maritimes or Ontario in those days were not the same as they are today with the large size of ridings, particularly in western Canada. Those ridings are what we might call big ridings in the big sky country. Some ridings are hundreds of miles in size. Even with paved roads and instant communication by telephone, 47 days may not be enough. I want those members to have an opportunity to consider the 47 days.
I suggest that other things could be done to the bill which would make the 47 days reasonable and would allow the electorate to be well informed. We are not only here to please ourselves and to be fair to all candidates. We are supposed to be fair to Canadians and to let them consider what each party is advocating and what is the philosophy of each party, and to provide them with a reasonable time in which to make up their minds.
Perhaps 47 days is the answer, but I think the government will find out that hon. members from large rural ridings have other ideas relating to the 47 days which may make the 47 days acceptable to all. The publication of the results of the opinion polls relates to the 47 days; whether or not the results of such polls will be published. There are two acts to amend the Canada Elections Act in that regard. There are a number of ideas about which hon. members have felt strongly enough to propose bills dealing with individual changes. Surely they must all be considered. Surely the opinion and the report of the Chief Electoral Officer must be considered. The Speech from the Throne and the attitude of the Prime Minister and his government toward major changes must be considered. They relate to the 47 days as well.
We should not be discussing this matter today; the bill should not be here at this time. We should be talking about the bankruptcy bill or something which is important to the country, rather than wasting the time of the House as we are doing today with this bill. There are acts regarding deposits, partisan poll officers and the representation of parties at polls to be considered. This 47 days as opposed to 60 days will make a difference as to whether or not these things will be possible, whether or not injustices will be involved. There is the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act and byelections preceding redistribution. This 47 days will have a lot to do with those bills, as well as with the mobile polling stations under the Canada Elections Act. If there are a couple of mobile polling stations in a 500-mile riding, I wonder how much the candidates can cover in 47 days. I am referring to many areas in western Canada or, for that matter, in the north.
What about the use of contributions, limiting them to federal uses? Well, I apologize for that one. It should not be included in here, because it has nothing to do with the act under discussion.
The period of 47 days is related to campaigning by non-residents and to permanent voters' lists. Those matters have a great deal to do with this particular piece of legislation. Many hon. members on all sides of the House have taken a look, or would like to contemplate, the potential of a permanent voters' list. This might make this legislation palatable to those with huge rural ridings. It can be done in many ways. The Australians have one system, but there are various ways in which it can be handled.
As I suggested, there were comments in the Speech from the Throne which proposed major changes. Also there was the speech in Winnipeg by the Prime Minister reiterating them as recently as last Monday, We know that the report of the Chief Electoral Officer is due in September. There is a raft of bills dealing with the Canada Elections Act, yet we have a little bill before us indicating limiting an electoral campaign to 47 days and stating that the list will no longer be printed. How can we deal with those matters in a vacuum without contemplating all other potential changes, ideas or concepts which might be very useful or interesting? Perhaps when we see the rest of the legislation it will be entirely possible that we may have a circumstance where 47 days will not be the ideal time. It may
June 5, 1981

be that there will be an all-party agreement that, perhaps, with this change and that change to the Elections Act we could conduct a proper federal election. This would be an election that would be fair to all Canadians. It would ensure that they have their information and that the examination would be conducted in the same time as that established in many provinces. Perhaps 35 days would be equally acceptable, I do not know. 1 do know that this bill should not be before us now because of the vast changes which will come about in the election process in this country when this bill comes into effect.
When we talk about the potential of proportional representation, I connect it to the question of a 47-day election campaign. An election is called, and 47 days later the voting takes place. If there is any form of proportional representation which falls into this category, it really means there will be two elections. It takes probably a week or two to get on the list on the basis of proportional representation; and, depending on the system used, a separate voting may be required within the election to determine who will be on the proportional list. This may require that a party convention be called, or it may mean that some form of primary election will have be held, as is the case in the United States. Under these circumstances, obviously, 47 days simply will not suffice, since at least two weeks of those 47 days will have been used up in order to determine who the proportional representation candidates are.
With that hanging over our heads, I wonder why we are even contemplating 47 days until we know what the rest of the package will be and whether 47 days will have anything to do with it at all. Yet this government brings in this measure to be debated on a lazy Friday afternoon. We are required to talk about it while the government does not understand that it should not be before us. Surely to goodness there is not that much poverty of mind and wisdom on the government benches that they cannot realize the implications of some of the legislation which should be before this House.

Canada Elections Act
before it is said to me "Let us have the 47-day provision." I want to deal with the total picture.
I could not possibly vote for this bill at this point in time, even though I find myself generally in agreement with the 47-day provision. speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am glad I had the opportunity to clear up the process with you before speaking on this bill, both earlier and during the few minutes in the House.
To me, this bill parallels the fill in the Ontario weekly newspapers, and that is what it is. It is fill. It does not really attack the problem of the Elections Act. We are talking about 47 days versus 59 days. The consequence of this 47 days will be the erosion of the democratic process in this country. Basically it gives the incumbent an advantage. Since the government has a majority, it would give the government an advantage. I have to state right here and now that 1 cannot support 47 days. I will give Your Honour more reasons as I go on.
The bill is totally incomplete. It does not cover anything. In my riding, I have a microcosm of Canada. I have urban development, I have an industrial area, and I have a large rural area which makes up the largest part of my riding. My first election campaign took me 365 days. Now I am being asked to cut my next election down from 64 days, which we happened to have the last time, to 47 days. I do not think there is any way that I could go back and be re-elected under these conditions. I will have had to work at it the four years I will have been here-something like 1,500 days.
There is just a little side point, one little item, which is missing from this bill. We talk about 321 members who will have 47 days the next time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext: That is right!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Those hon. members will no longer be known as backbenchers. They will be known as the 47-day upper
benchers sitting in the gallery because there will be nowhere else to put them, or else we will all crowd in together when we come in for a vote. I hope we are given 47 days to vote.
Another point which I feel was left out of the bill is that volunteers in a campaign who are supposed to raise money have no longer been given a challenge. They have a great opportunity to go and raise all the money they want. But now, the government wants control of the election, so it gives back the money, and I disagree with that. I think perhaps the new candidates should be helped out, but the incumbents should raise their own money. They have about 1,500 days in which to raise money while they are in office. If they have done a good job, they will receive all kinds of money to run their campaign. If they are not re-elected, that is their own fault.
There should be some method of improving the electoral lists because one of the major problems of our campaign offices is dealing with people who did not get on the list. I have an unusual situation, particularly in part of my rural riding where people are not allowed to register when they come to vote. Half of those people in my rural riding can register when they come to vote and the other half cannot, and they must be enumerated. There is no geographic difference. These people live on farms where the enumerator does not get around. These people are out in the fields and the wife is out to work. It just does not work.
Perhaps 47 days might be practicable if people were allowed to register at the polls. During this debate some members have suggested that a permanent list would solve the problem of 47 days. I shudder at the thought of a permanent list, and I will tell you why. It is because we would create a whole new bureaucracy right across Canada, in 281 constituencies. I cannot accept that. I believe that 59 days is a minimum we can deal with.
One little point which is missing in this bill is the matter of a deposit. In 1867 it cost $200 to put one's name on the line to get elected. On a relative dollar basis, with the inflation we are experiencing, that deposit should be $20,000, but maybe I will cut it down and say that we should be required to put in $2,000. It is just a little extra point that is missing in this bill.
Another little point is with regard to the hours. It was tough for the people in Vancouver to find out that the Liberals had won the election while they were still voting. There should be some adaptation made there. I really feel strongly about that. There are several private members' bills but-

speechtext: Vote Liberal!

speechtext:
-it is just a point. We have to look at this total package. It is simply not enough. This bill is not doing anything for the country. We are not representing our constituents if all we tell them in this bill is that there will be 12 days fewer than the last time around. I think that is totally unfair. Basically, it is fine. If I had a district to represent such as downtown Toronto, where there is all these highrises, it would be simple. All one does is to go up and down elevators. One goes up the elevators and then one walks all the way down. I
June 5, 1981

do have some apartment buildings in my constituency, and it is a lot of work. However, I could cover that in 47 days.
What this bill will do to my constituency is turn over 80 per cent of my rural constituents into second-class citizens, and they are the ones who are the guts of the country. They are the true entrepreneurs. They are the people who started this country. They are second, third, fourth and fifth generation farmers. Even 59 days is not long enough for us to see them all. How much less would we see them in 47 days?
One matter which has been touched on in this debate is proportional representation, a matter which has been missed in this 47-day bill. I would suggest that if we are going to talk about proportional representation, we should look at the whole of government service. Let us start electing our senators, perhaps for life, if so desired. However, they should be elected as proportional representatives. We have a great big area at the east end of this building. We could be doing a lot more productive things with this area than what 1 have seen in the two years I have been here.
I would have one suggestion on the 47 days proposal. If we knew for sure that there will be no election for at least four years, perhaps we could accept the 47 days, because incumbents and new candidates would have enough time in three or four years to build up an organization and to build up their image. Perhaps when the bill goes to committee an amendment could be made which would provide that for elections which are four years apart, an electoral campaign of only 47 days would be allowed, but for elections which come sooner, that is, snap elections, the length of time of the campaign would remain at 59 days. That way, there would be an opportunity for good candidates to be picked, and if there had to be last-minute choices, there would be better people to choose from. All parties have the same problem of finding candidates when there is a snap election. Your Honour knows that. That is probably how I was elected the first time; they did not have time to look around. However, they are happy with me now. Personally, I think I can do it in 47 days, but I feel sorry for the new guy who comes in and does not have the same opportunity that I had with 365 days.
1 have another possible amendment which could also be discussed in committee. Why not do away with elections altogether and just let the Gallup poll take care of it? That seems to be how we do it anyway. Let us make it equal so that we in the opposition have the same opportunity as the government. An election act and its subparts deal with the rights of Canadian voters to choose their peer group, which is their jury. In the case of federal politics, that peer group or jury is to be found in this chamber. Any attempt to alter the relationship between the individual voter and his or her right or obligation to choose who represents him or her is a matter which should be undertaken only after very serious thought, and only in the context of our particular form of parliament.
I stand here in this House with a sense of foreboding about the consequences of the proposed change. I think that perhaps the principle which is really basic to that sense of foreboding begins with the notion of process. As we debated the Constitution, I felt that it was most unfortunate that it was a piece of legislation introduced to this chamber by a government, by a small group of members of this House, who had a long-term vested interest. I wonder what the constitutional resolution would have looked like had we had an advisory group consisting of knowledgeable Canadians with no vested interest in this particular source of power called the House of Commons of Canada, to give us ideas and advice. If an advisory group had come up with ideas, suggestions and potential legislation for the House, after which legislation had been brought forward which all members had an opportunity to debate freely, and on which to vote freely, perhaps it would have been better.
I had the same feeling about this proposed electoral change. I think it behooves us in this House to begin an examination of this proposed change with the following in mind: let us assume that government members, members of the Liberal Party, like sitting on that side of the House and like the responsibility of forming a cabinet and deciding which legislation comes forward. But when they propose a particular piece of electoral reform, can they be objective and dispassionate about the consequences of that proposed reform, or is re-election to this chamber uppermost in their minds? I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that is a great deal to ask of any man or woman. It is far too much to ask of the present cabinet, far too much.
